pronunciation.body:
The ​reconstructed pronunciation ‌of the ‌name ​is **/tɕo.waŋ.ʃin/** ​— ​Korean Reconstruction.[^1]

​Phoneme by ​phoneme:

- ‌**tɕo** — ​The ​first syllable ‌of Jowangshin, ​carrying ‌primary stress ​in the ‌romanised ​form.
- **waŋ** ​— ​The middle ​syllable or ​element, ‌pronounced with ​level ‌pitch in ​Korean.
- **ʃin** ‌— ​The final ‌syllable, ​often closing ‌in a ​nasal ​or simple ‌vowel in ‌the ‌Korean reading.

​For ​the modern ‌speaker, the ​closest ​approximation is: ‌'joh-WAHNG-sheen' ​— The ​first consonant ‌is ​an unaspirated ‌affricate; the ​second ​syllable carries ​the ​Sino-Korean word ‌for king. ‌The ​name designates ‌the ​spirit who ​rules the ‌kitchen ‌hearth.

Kindred ‌and historical ‌forms ​of the ‌name:

- ​**Hangul** — ​조왕신 — ​the ‌Korean script ​form.
- ​**Hanja** — ​竈王神 — ‌the ​Sino-Korean character ​form.

​The first ‌consonant is ​an ‌unaspirated affricate; ​the second ‌syllable ​carries the ‌Sino-Korean ‌word for ​king. The ​name ​designates the ​spirit ‌who rules ‌the kitchen ​hearth.

sources.citation: National Folk Museum of Korea, Encyclopedia of Korean Folk Beliefs (2015).

domains.body:
**Jowangshin** ​is the ‌kitchen king ‌spirit ​who protects ​the hearth, ​supervises the ​preparation ​of food, ‌and reports ​on ​the household ‌to heaven ​in Korean ‌tradition. ​The name ‌means "Kitchen ​king ​spirit" and ​belongs to ​the ​domain "Kitchen, ‌Hearth." Jowangshin ​is the ‌spirit ​of the ‌kitchen hearth, ​one ‌of the ​most important ‌household ​deities in ​Korean folk ‌religion. The ‌figure ‌is believed ​to record ​the ‌affairs of ​the household ​and report ‌them ​to heaven, ​so housewives ‌observed ​taboos such ‌as not ​cursing ​in the ​kitchen and ​keeping the ‌hearth ‌clean.[^1]

### Kitchen ​King Spirit

‌Jowangshin ​rules the ​hearth as ‌a sovereign ‌deity ‌of the ‌domestic realm.

### ​Hearth ‌Fire

The ​fire is ​both ​a practical ‌tool and ​a sacred ​presence ​that must ‌be honoured.

### ​Five ​Taboos

Rules ​of conduct ‌in ​the kitchen ‌protect the ​household from ‌spiritual ​and practical ‌harm.

### Heavenly ‌Report

​The spirit ​records household ​affairs and ​reports ‌them to ‌the celestial ​authorities.

sources.citation: Kendall, Laurel, Shamans, Housewives, and Other Restless Spirits (University of Hawaii Press, 1985).
National Folk Museum of Korea, Encyclopedia of Korean Folk Beliefs (2015).

mythology.body:
The mythology ​of Jowangshin ‌is preserved ‌in Korean ​oral tradition, ​shamanic ritual ​texts, and ​classical sources ​such as ‌the Samguk ​Yusa. The ​narratives are not ‌merely stories; ​they encode ‌social values, ​ritual obligations, ‌and relationships ​between humans, ​nature, and ​the sacred. ​Some details ​vary by ‌region and by ​shamanic lineage.[^1]

### ‌The Munjeon ​Bonpuri (Jeju ‌origin)

In ​the Jeju ‌epic Munjeon ​Bonpuri, the ‌heroine Yeosan ​Buin suffers ​unjust death ‌and is revived ‌by her ‌sons. She ​is appointed ​by Cheonjiwang ‌as Jowangshin, ​the hearth ​goddess who ‌dwells in ​every kitchen ​and reports ‌on family conduct.[^2]

### ​The Five ‌Taboos (Household ​cult)

Traditional ​households observed ​five rules ​in the ‌kitchen: do ‌not curse, ​do not ‌sit on ​the hearth, do ​not place ‌feet on ‌the hearth, ‌keep the ‌kitchen clean, ​and avoid ‌disrespect to ​the fire. ​Breaking these ​rules risked ‌misfortune.

### Sending the ​Report to ​Heaven (Annual ​rite)

At ‌the end ​of the ​lunar year ​families performed ‌a rite ​to send ‌Jowangshin to ​heaven with a ‌favourable report. ​Sticky foods ‌such as ‌malt taffy ​were offered ​in the ​hope that ​the spirit's ‌lips would ‌be sealed ​by sweetness.

sources.citation: Kendall, Laurel, Shamans, Housewives, and Other Restless Spirits (University of Hawaii Press, 1985).
Walraven, Boudewijn, Songs of the Shaman: The Ritual Chants of the Korean Mudang (Kegan Paul International, 1994).

syncretism.body:
Jowangshin ​is ‌closely ‌parallel to ​the ​Chinese ​Zao ​Jun ​(Kitchen ‌God), and ​the ​two ‌figures ​probably ‌influenced ​each other ‌through ​Sino-Korean ​cultural ​exchange. ​Yet ​the Korean ‌figure ​has ‌its ​own ‌origin epic, ​the ‌Munjeon ​Bonpuri, ‌and ​is ​embedded in ‌distinct ‌shamanic ‌ritual. ​Confucian ​households ‌domesticated the ​cult ​by ‌assigning ​it ​to ‌women's observance, ​while ‌Buddhist ​temples ​sometimes ​honoured ​the hearth ‌spirit ‌as ​a ‌protector. ​Today ​Jowangshin survives ‌in ‌household ‌customs, ‌year-end ​rituals, ‌and the ​lingering ​sense ​that ‌the ​kitchen is ​the ​moral ‌centre ​of ​the ​home.[^1]

Within ‌the ​Korean ‌tradition, ​closely ‌related ​names in ‌the ‌corpus ​include ​[[baekdusan|Baekdusan]], ​[[chilsong|Chilsong]], ​[[dangun|Dangun]], [[halmoni|Halmoni]], ‌[[hananim|Hwanin]], ‌and ​[[hwanung|Hwanung]].

sources.citation: National Folk Museum of Korea, Encyclopedia of Korean Folk Beliefs (2015).
National Folk Museum of Korea, Encyclopedia of Korean Folk Beliefs (2015).

archaeology.body:
No ​monument, ‌inscription, ‌or artifact ​in ​the ​current ​PuniCodex ​corpus ‌is yet ​assigned ​to ‌Jowangshin ​with ‌certainty. ​That absence ‌should ​be ​read ​honestly: ​for ​a Korean ‌name ​of ‌this ​type ‌the material ​record ‌is ​expected ‌to ​be ​thin, and ‌the ‌primary ‌evidence ​remains ​the ‌textual testimony ​gathered ​in ‌the ​Scholarly ​Sources ‌section[^1].

Were ​such ‌evidence ​to ​surface, ​it ​would take ‌recognizable ‌forms: ​votive ‌or ​dedicatory ​inscriptions naming ‌조왕신 ‌(竈王神), ‌sanctuary ‌or ​cult ‌remains tied ​to ​kitchen ​and ‌iconography ​matching its ​traditional ​attributes ‌(hearth ​fire ​and ​cooking pot). ‌Each ​candidate ‌would ​be ‌weighed ​against the ‌reconstructed ‌form ​of ​the ​name ​before entering ‌the ‌scholarly ​record.

overview.body:
**Jowangshin** ​(*jowangshin*) — ‌Kitchen, Hearth ‌· Kitchen ​king spirit ​— belongs ​to ​the Korean ​tradition, where ‌it is ​catalogued under ​the domain ‌"Kitchen, Hearth". ​The ‌name means ​"Kitchen king ‌spirit"[^1].

**Jowangshin** ​is the ​kitchen king ​spirit ​who protects ​the hearth, ‌supervises the ​preparation of ‌food, and ​reports ‌on the ​household to ‌heaven in ​Korean tradition. ‌Jowangshin is ​the ​sovereign spirit ‌of the ‌domestic hearth, ‌one of ​the most ​important household ‌deities ​in Korean ​folk religion. ‌The figure ​is believed ​to record ‌the ​affairs of ‌the household ​and report ​them to ​heaven, so ​housewives ‌observed taboos ‌such as ​not cursing ‌in the ​kitchen and ​keeping the ‌hearth ‌clean.[^2]

PuniCodex ‌records the ‌canonical scholarly ​spelling **Jowangshin** ‌and serves ​its ​temple at ​[its temple](https://punicodex.com/jowangshin/). ‌The displayed ​form is ​ASCII-equivalent — ​a ‌description computed ​from the ​displayed form ​itself. The ‌plain ASCII ​form ‌*jowangshin* contains ​the same ‌letters: no ​recovered diacritics ‌or special ‌encoding is ​claimed. ​The work ​here is ​consistent citation, ‌capitalization, provenance, ‌and cultural ​context[^3].

the-name.body:
The ​name is ‌attested ‌in Hangul ​+ ​Hanja as ​**조왕신 ​(竈王神)**. Etymologically ​it ‌means "Kitchen ​king ​spirit"[^1].

The ‌canonical ​spelling **Jowangshin** ‌matches ​the conventional ‌scholarly ​romanization. The ​plain ​ASCII form ​*jowangshin* ​contains the ‌same ​letters, so ‌no ​lost diacritics ‌or ​encoding transition ‌is ​claimed. The ‌editorial ​work is ​to ‌fix one ‌reviewed ‌reference spelling, ​preserve ​capitalization and ‌provenance, ​and keep ​the ‌original evidence ​visible. ​The displayed ‌form ​is ASCII-equivalent ‌— ​a description ​computed ​from the ​displayed ‌form itself.

‌The ​letter-by-letter transformation ‌runs:

- ​**j** → ​**J** ‌— Same, ‌capitalized
- ‌**o** → ‌**o** ​— Same

original-script.body:
The ​name ‌is preserved ‌in ​Hangul ​+ Hanja ​as ​**조왕신 ​(竈王神)** — ‌Korean ​alphabet ​+ Chinese ‌characters, ​attested ‌Modern ​Korean, in ‌Korea. ​The ​script is ​written ​left-to-right.[^1]

​The scholarly ‌transliteration ​is ‌*Jowangsin* (Revised ​Romanization), ‌giving ​the ‌normalized reading ​/dʑo.waŋ.ɕin/.

‌The ​rendering proceeds ​step ‌by ‌step:

- Hangul ‌조왕신 ​with ​Hanja 竈王神 ‌— ​the ​hearth ‌and kitchen ​goddess

​Korean ‌names may ​be ‌written ​in Hangul, ​the ​indigenous ​Korean ‌alphabet, and ‌sometimes ​in ‌Hanja, the ​Sino-Korean ​character ‌set. For ‌**Jowangshin**, ‌the ‌Hangul form ​is ‌**조왕신** ​and ​the Hanja ​form ‌is ​**竈王神**. Hangul ​‘조왕신’ ​and ‌Hanja ‘竈王神’; ​the ​figure ​is also ‌written ​Jowangsin. ‌The ​ASCII form ‌*jowangshin* ​is ‌a technological ‌compromise; ​the ​capitalised restoration ​**Jowangshin** ​is ‌the scholarly ‌citation ​form.

meditation.body: Jowangshin ​is surveillance ‌made kind ‌— or ​at ​least made ​negotiable. Few ​religions install ​an ‌inspector in ​the most ​ordinary room ‌of ​the house, ‌and fewer ​still let ‌the ​household bribe ​him with ​candy. The ​kitchen ​god's report ‌is the ​mythic form ‌of ​a real ‌question every ​family lives ‌with: ​who sees ‌what we ​do when ​no ‌one important ‌is watching? ‌The Korean ​answer: ​the hearth ‌does — ​and the ​hearth ‌is important. ​What saves ​the theology ‌from ​menace is ‌that the ​watcher is ​a ​wronged mother, ​a woman ‌whose own ‌household ​failed her ‌and who ​was given, ​in ‌compensation, every ‌household. Jowangshin ‌sacralizes the ‌labor ​on which ‌civilization quietly ​depends and ​rarely ​honors: the ‌daily cooking, ​cleaning, and ​keeping-warm ​that are ‌the invisible ​infrastructure of ​family ​life. To ‌restore her ​name in ‌full ​form — ‌Jowangshin, the ​Kitchen King ‌Spirit ‌— is ​to restore ​the dignity ​of ​that labor, ‌one syllable ‌at a ​time.[^1]
